protections: Runtime values reach SQL only as `?` placeholders rendered client-side by escapeValue (single-quote wrapping plus quote doubling), because ClickHouseAdapter uses substituteParameters as the sole rendering step - packages/clickhouse/src/core/utils.ts:1-32, packages/clickhouse/src/core/adapters/clickhouse-adapter.ts:42-51

Raw SQL text (expr.raw(), .raw(), .having(), the sql tag, field-level sql expressions) is inserted verbatim and treated as developer-trusted code - packages/clickhouse/src/core/formatters/sql-formatter.ts:45-49, packages/clickhouse/src/dataset/sql-tag.ts:48-51

Interpolated identifiers are trusted everywhere except the withScalar alias, which is checked against ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; the datasets package has its own validateSQLIdentifier/quoteSQLIdentifier for generated SQL - packages/clickhouse/src/core/query-builder.ts:367-371, packages/datasets/src/sql-utils.ts:23-43

Dataset and metric filter field names are whitelisted against the dataset contract before SQL generation - packages/datasets/src/executor.ts:82-86, packages/serve/src/semantic/datasets/utils/dataset-query-validation.ts:38-50

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Object/array values are developer-supplied structured data and a JSON payload is not a value shape ClickHouse columns accept, so the fallback branch is read as a convenience rather than a user-data route.
The SQL text is developer-authored; a `?` inside a quoted literal or comment is a coding error and the placeholder/parameter count check throws instead of executing.
Scalar expressions are developer-authored CTE definitions built from literals and column references, and rendering their parameters at build time is deliberate so the CTE text matches the expression.
expr.raw() and .raw() values are documented raw-SQL escape hatches, and the project's where tests pin the exact flat SQL, so a solver can argue composition is the caller's responsibility.
having() and .raw() take raw SQL text by design and several fragments are already documented as joined with AND, so the fragment text is treated as the caller's syntax.

buildLogical already parenthesises every child expression, so the expression is unambiguous on its own; the remaining risk appears only when a caller mixes it into a flat sequence, which is the caller's composition.
fn() names are developer constants written in application code, not request input, so no runtime allowlist is expected.
CTE aliases are developer-chosen identifiers written at the call site, and the sibling withScalar path already enforces an identifier regex, so the API looks consistently trusted.
Aggregate aliases and columns are typed by schema-derived TypeScript template literals, so they are compile-time-trusted identifiers rather than runtime data.

Measure-level filter values are developer-authored in the measure definition and the project spec calls custom SQL in field definitions trusted code, so this literal renderer is read as a second, developer-only implementation.

This is a byte-for-byte copy of the datasets renderer fed from the same developer-authored measure definitions, so the same trusted-code argument applies and a solver who fixed the datasets copy sees no reason to open the second one.
Format strings, timezones and intervals are code-level constants passed to SELECT-expression helpers, and ClickHouse requires them inside literal or INTERVAL syntax.
rawAs()/selectExpr() are the documented select-expression escape hatch and the alias is a developer-chosen label, not request data.
inSubquery/inTable values are documented as raw subquery and table SQL strings, not as bound values, and the operator names say so.
The published fix re-documented the sql tag as an intentional raw-SQL authoring API and the project pins verbatim interpolation, so it is treated as developer code rather than a to-be-escaped sink.
Table names, join aliases, order/limit-by columns and select expressions all originate from schema-typed columns or builder arguments, and every request-facing path whitelists field names first.

masking: T4 is masked by T3: withScalar renders its own parameters at build time (analytics.ts:26) and the executor substitutes the whole query again (executor.ts:30-32), so a `?` inside a scalar literal only corrupts SQL through the lexical split; a test written after the scanner lands will not see T4 at all.

T11/T12 only surface through T3 when a measure-filter literal itself contains `?`: the datasets renderer pastes the literal into the same SQL string that is later handed to substituteParameters (datasets/src/query-planner.ts:68 -> datasets/src/executor.ts:265-269 -> clickhouse-adapter.ts:43), so the cross-package literal gap is hidden while the clickhouse escaper is the only thing under review.

conflicts.what: The natural escaping fix for T1 (double backslashes, keep quote doubling) has to be duplicated in T11/T12, but datasets.test.ts:624-632 pins the exact measure-filter SQL `(status = 'completed')`; routing measure filters through placeholders or rewriting them instead of escaping breaks that pinned output and the sum()-takes-a-column-string contract.

Blanket-parenthesising composed fragments to close T5-T7 changes the exact SQL that the escaping suite pins (query-builder.where.test.ts:33, 307, 370, 414, 449 and query-builder-analytics.test.ts:69-78), so the composition guard must wrap only fragments carrying top-level AND/OR and leave condition values and flat sequences untouched.

Extending the escaping rule to the sql tag closes T16 on paper but breaks the test-pinned verbatim interpolation (sql-tag.test.ts:17-22) and the documented trusted-SQL authoring route (DATASETS_AND_METRICS_SPEC.md:890-891); any rule for T1/T2 must stop at the documented raw-SQL entry points.

fairness_risks: The sql tagged template must keep inserting interpolated strings verbatim (sql-tag.test.ts:17-22) and custom sql in field definitions is declared trusted code (DATASETS_AND_METRICS_SPEC.md:891); a security rule that escapes every interpolated string contradicts a documented, test-pinned authoring API.
expr.raw(), .raw() and .having() fragments must stay byte-identical (query-builder-analytics.test.ts:69-78, query-builder.where.test.ts:427-434); blanket escaping or blanket wrapping breaks them.

Quote doubling for single quotes is pinned (query-builder.where.test.ts:33, 307): switching the quote escape to a backslash form for T1 breaks existing output, so backslash doubling must be added on top of doubling.
Flat AND/OR sequences are pinned as intentional SQL (query-builder.where.test.ts:275, 291), so the composition fix must not parenthesise ordinary conditions.
Filtered-measure SQL is pinned exactly (datasets.test.ts:624-632), so T11/T12 must add backslash handling without changing the simple-value rendering.
formatDateTime output is pinned with single-quoted format and timezone literals (sql-expressions.test.ts:43-56), so any escaping in T13 must leave the common case unchanged.
substituteParameters must return parameterless SQL untouched (utils.ts:17-19); a scanner must not rewrite SQL that has no parameters, otherwise rawQuery and every parameterless builder query change.

Refused input shapes that legitimate uses need: rendering object/array values is the only route for a developer to bind JSON today (utils.ts:11-13), null must still render, and `?` characters legitimately appear in LIKE patterns and comments of developer SQL.

design.why: Five independent groups, each needing a different judgement rather than a different spelling of one. T1 is the reported anchor (escapeValue's string literal) with no dismissal; T3 is the lexical placeholder split in the same file, dismissed as developer-authored SQL, and needs a real scanner that understands quotes, comments and heredocs; T5 is the composition group where a fragment with top-level AND/OR is spliced into a flat sequence, dismissed as a documented raw-SQL escape hatch and punished by pinned exact SQL if over-hardened; T9 is the identifier sink for CTE aliases in a different feature module, dismissed as developer-chosen names and easy to miss because the sibling withScalar alias is already validated; T11 is the second, duplicated literal renderer in another package, dismissed as trusted developer measure filters and invisible to anyone who only audits the clickhouse escaper. Deepseek-type groups are T3, T9 and T11 (absent protection plus a dismissal), and T5 is the clean mimo-type group (coupled exact-SQL), so both model failure modes are probed; the groups span three packages and five modules, and the distance-0 anchor keeps the task solvable while the far sites do the stacking work. T16 and T17 are left out of the design: T16 is the project's documented raw-SQL authoring API and would be unfair to require, and T17's request paths are all whitelisted before SQL generation.
